title: Akhenaten's Revolution
description: A pharaoh who tried to make Egypt worship the sun disk alone, and how Egypt erased him

concepts.title: The Aten and the Horizon City
concepts.contentHtml:
Amenhotep IV came to the throne of Egypt in about 1353 BCE, son of the long-reigning Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty. (Egyptian regnal dates carry an uncertainty of a decade or more; many books give c. 1353 to 1336 BCE.) In his first years he began building temples at Karnak, the great sanctuary of Amun at Thebes, to a different god: the Aten, the visible disk of the sun. The Aten was not new, since earlier texts treat it as an aspect of the sun god. What was new was the king's insistence on it.

In about his fifth year the king changed his name to Akhenaten, usually translated "effective for the Aten", and founded a new capital on unoccupied ground in Middle Egypt, roughly halfway between Thebes and Memphis. He called it Akhetaten, "Horizon of the Aten"; the site is now known as Amarna. Boundary stelae cut into the surrounding cliffs fix the city's limits and record his wish to be buried there.

The Aten was shown not as an animal or a human figure but as a disk whose rays end in small hands, some holding the ankh sign of life to the faces of the king and his queen, Nefertiti. Its names were written inside cartouches, like a king's, and its temples were open to the sky. Workmen chiseled the name of Amun off monuments across the country, and in some inscriptions even the plural word "gods" was erased. Art changed too: the royal family appears with elongated faces and full bellies, kissing and playing with their daughters, in scenes no earlier pharaoh had allowed.

concepts.title: The Great Hymn and the Monotheism Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
The fullest statement of the new religion is the Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in the tomb prepared at Amarna for the courtier Ay, who would later become pharaoh. It praises the sun as sole maker and sustainer of everything: the chick that cries out inside its egg, the fish in the river, the lands of Syria and Kush, and peoples whose languages and skins the god made different. One standard translation addresses the Aten as "sole god, like whom there is no other". The hymn also insists that only the king truly knows the god: there is no other who knows you, it says, except your son Akhenaten.

Since the American Egyptologist James Henry Breasted wrote in the early 20th century, readers have noticed resemblances to Psalm 104, where lions roam at night and ships go on the sea. Whether the psalm descends from the hymn or simply draws on a shared stock of Near Eastern nature praise is unresolved. Sigmund Freud went much further in Moses and Monotheism (1939), speculating that Moses was an Egyptian follower of the Aten; no evidence supports this.

Was it monotheism? Scholars such as Erik Hornung and Jan Assmann treat it as the first known attempt to replace the gods with one god. Others stress its limits. The Aten was worshiped through the royal family, which formed a kind of triad with the god, and houses at Amarna had shrines showing the king and queen. Excavations there, including the workmen's village, also turned up amulets of household gods such as Bes and Taweret, so ordinary people did not give up the old gods. Many therefore prefer terms such as monolatry or an exclusive court cult: one god worshiped, the others suppressed rather than disproved.

concepts.title: Erasure and the Boy King's New Name
concepts.contentHtml:
Akhenaten died in about his 17th regnal year. The succession that followed is one of the murkiest stretches of Egyptian history: one or two short-lived rulers, known as Smenkhkare and Neferneferuaten, probably reigned, and some Egyptologists identify the second with Nefertiti herself. Then a boy of about eight or nine took the throne as Tutankhaten, "living image of the Aten". Within a few years he had become Tutankhamun, "living image of Amun", and his wife Ankhesenpaaten had become Ankhesenamun. The court left Amarna, which was soon abandoned.

A Restoration Stela set up at Karnak in Tutankhamun's name describes the temples fallen into ruin and the gods turning their backs on Egypt, and announces the reopening of their shrines. Under Horemheb, a general who became king after Ay, the Aten temples were dismantled. Their small, standard-sized blocks, called talatat, were packed as fill into new pylons at Karnak, which by accident preserved tens of thousands of them for modern excavators.

The king list carved under Seti I at Abydos, and another in a Ramesside tomb at Saqqara, jump straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb, leaving out Akhenaten, his successors, Tutankhamun and Ay. A Ramesside court record refers to Akhenaten without naming him, by a phrase translated roughly as "that damned one of Akhetaten". The memory came back only in modern times: the cuneiform Amarna Letters, a diplomatic archive, turned up at the site in 1887, and Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's largely intact tomb in 1922. The boy king is famous today partly because his small tomb, though entered by robbers soon after the burial, was later buried under debris and escaped the plundering that emptied other royal tombs.

title: Gods of the Roman State
description: Sol Invictus, the Christmas question, and how Rome's public cults lost the state

concepts.title: Aurelian and the Unconquered Sun
concepts.contentHtml:
Roman religion was a public business. Magistrates sacrificed for the safety of the state, priestly colleges kept the calendar, and the gods were expected to return favor for correct cult. The sun already had a place in it, and invictus, "unconquered", was an epithet given to several gods, including Hercules and Mithras. An earlier experiment had gone badly: the emperor Elagabalus (r. 218 to 222), hereditary priest of the sun god of Emesa in Syria, raised his god above Jupiter and was murdered.

Aurelian (r. 270 to 275) came to power in the middle of a crisis. Within a few years he defeated the breakaway Palmyrene realm of Queen Zenobia (272 to 273) and the Gallic Empire in the west (274), reuniting the empire. In 274 CE he dedicated a large new temple to Sol in Rome, reportedly paid for with eastern spoils, created a new college of senatorial priests, the pontifices Solis, and founded games for the god every four years. Some of his coins call Sol "lord of the Roman Empire".

Older scholarship described this as a Syrian cult imposed on Rome. Steven Hijmans and others argue instead that Aurelian's Sol was a traditional Roman god given new prominence; the question is still debated. Sol remained on imperial coins into the reign of Constantine, whose coinage honored "the Unconquered Sun, companion" of the emperor until about 320. In 321 Constantine ordered courts and city workshops to rest on "the venerable day of the Sun", a law that suited both sun worshipers and Christians, who already met on that day.

concepts.title: The 25 December Question
concepts.contentHtml:
A popular claim holds that the church put Christmas on 25 December to replace the pagan birthday of Sol Invictus. The evidence is thinner than that, and more interesting. The key document is the Chronograph of 354, an illustrated almanac made for a wealthy Roman Christian. Its civil calendar marks 25 December as N(atalis) Invicti, "birthday of the Unconquered", with 30 chariot races. Its list of martyrs' feasts, which reflects Roman church practice as of about 336, opens with "25 December: Christ born in Bethlehem of Judea". That is the earliest firm evidence for Christmas on this date, and both entries sit in the same book.

The history of religions explanation, made influential by the German scholar Hermann Usener in the late 19th century, says the church chose the date to Christianize a popular sun festival, perhaps one founded by Aurelian. A gloss in a medieval Syriac manuscript says much the same. The calculation explanation, argued by Louis Duchesne and later Thomas Talley, says some early Christians dated Jesus's conception to 25 March, the date they also assigned to his death, and counted nine months forward. Some Christians in the East reached 6 January by similar reasoning from a different spring date.

Two cautions apply. No source earlier than 354 places a festival of Sol on 25 December, and no ancient source says Aurelian dedicated his temple on that day; the games of Sol in the same calendar fall in October. And the two theories need not exclude each other: a date reached by calculation could still have been welcomed because it competed with a solar feast. Scholars remain divided, and the honest answer is that the evidence does not settle it.

concepts.title: Victory Leaves the Senate House
concepts.contentHtml:
For nearly four centuries the Roman Senate met in the Curia before a statue of the goddess Victoria and her altar, set up by Augustus in 29 BCE after his victory at Actium. Senators offered incense there before debate. The Christian emperor Constantius II removed the altar in 357; it was later put back. In 382 the emperor Gratian removed it again and cut public funding for the Vestal Virgins and the old priesthoods. Around the same time the emperors stopped using the ancient priestly title pontifex maximus, though the exact date is argued.

In 384 the prefect of Rome, Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a senator and pagan priest, asked the young emperor Valentinian II in his third Relatio to restore the altar. His most quoted line pleads for tolerance: so great a mystery, he wrote, cannot be reached by one road alone. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, answered in two letters that a Christian emperor could not support idolatry, and Valentinian refused. Pagan senators found brief hope under the usurper Eugenius (392 to 394), but his defeat ended the matter.

Laws issued under Theodosius I in 391 and 392 banned sacrifice and then all pagan cult, even private household offerings. The great Serapeum of Alexandria was destroyed by Christians in 391 or 392. Enforcement was uneven; many temples stood for generations, became churches, or simply decayed. Popular dates for "the end" are shakier than they look. The claim that Theodosius abolished the Olympic Games in 393 rests on late sources, and the temple of Isis at Philae, which Procopius says was shut under Justinian in the 530s, may have had little active cult left by then.

title: Baal, Moloch and the Gods of Rivals
description: How the gods of neighbors and enemies were described, demonized and argued over

concepts.title: Baal: Storm Hero, Biblical Villain
concepts.contentHtml:
The word baʿal means "lord", "owner" or "husband" in the Semitic languages of the Levant, and it served as a title for many local gods. In the tablets of Ugarit on the Syrian coast (13th and early 12th centuries BCE), Baal is the young storm god Haddu, or Hadad, called "Rider of the Clouds". In the Baal Cycle he defeats Yam, the Sea, wins a palace, is swallowed by Mot, Death, and returns when his sister Anat destroys Mot, bringing back the rains. He is a hero of order and fertility, not a demon.

In the Hebrew Bible the picture is reversed: Baal is the rival above all others. Queen Jezebel, daughter of a king of Sidon, promotes his cult; King Ahab builds him a temple in Samaria; Elijah defeats his prophets in a contest of fire on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18); Jehu massacres his worshipers (2 Kings 10). The prophet Hosea imagines Israel calling its God "my husband" and no longer "my baal". Yet scholars also see borrowing. Psalm 68 calls Yahweh the one who rides on the clouds, and Isaiah 27:1 describes Leviathan as "the twisting serpent", the same phrase Ugaritic poets used of the sea monster Litan.

The rivalry shows in names. Saul's son Eshbaal (1 Chronicles 8:33) appears in the books of Samuel as Ish-bosheth, "man of shame", and Jonathan's son Meribbaal becomes Mephibosheth. Most scholars think later scribes swapped bosheth, "shame", for the offending divine title. The original names suggest that "baal" was once an acceptable title even for Israel's own God.

concepts.title: Moloch: A God or a Sacrifice?
concepts.contentHtml:
Biblical laws condemn making a son or daughter "pass through the fire" lammolek, traditionally translated "to Molech" (Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2 to 5). King Josiah is said to have defiled the Topheth in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom outside Jerusalem "so that no one would make a son or a daughter pass through fire as an offering to Molech" (2 Kings 23:10), and Jeremiah accuses Judeans of burning their children there. The valley's Hebrew name, Ge Hinnom, later gave Jewish and Christian tradition Gehenna, a word for hell.

In 1935 the German scholar Otto Eissfeldt proposed another reading. Punic inscriptions from North Africa use mlk as a technical term for a type of offering, so lammolek might mean "as a molk-offering", and there might never have been a god called Molech. Critics, including George Heider and John Day, reply that Leviticus speaks of people "prostituting themselves" after Molech, which suits a god, and they point to an underworld deity called Malik or Milku in older Near Eastern texts. A long-standing suggestion holds that scribes gave the name the vowels of bosheth, "shame", as with Ish-bosheth. The question is still open.

The famous picture of a bronze idol with outstretched arms and a fire inside comes from later writers, not the Bible. The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE) describes a bronze statue of "Kronos" at Carthage whose hands sloped toward the ground, so that a child placed on them rolled into a pit of fire. Medieval Jewish commentators added the hollow, heated bronze figure, and Gustave Flaubert's novel Salammbô (1862) fixed the image for modern readers.

concepts.title: The Carthage Tophet: Evidence Both Ways
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1921 a sacred precinct was found near the ancient harbors of Carthage in Tunisia; it is called the Tophet, after the biblical word. Excavations in the 1920s, and an American project led by Lawrence Stager from 1975 to 1980, found thousands of urns holding the cremated bones of infants and young children, sometimes of lambs or kids instead, many beneath carved stone markers. The precinct was used from about the 8th century BCE until Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. Stager estimated that as many as 20,000 urns may have been buried there between 400 and 200 BCE. Similar precincts exist at Phoenician colonies in Sicily, Sardinia and elsewhere in Tunisia, but none has been securely identified in Phoenicia itself.

The case for sacrifice: Greek and Roman writers, including Diodorus and Plutarch, describe Carthaginians offering children to Baal Hammon, whom Greeks called Kronos, and Diodorus says 200 children of noble families were sacrificed during a military crisis in 310 BCE. The markers dedicate a vowed gift to Baal Hammon and the goddess Tanit "because he heard his voice", language suited to an offering rather than a grave. Animals appear as substitutes, which makes little sense in an ordinary cemetery.

The case against: the classical writers were Carthage's enemies, and a special cemetery for infants who died naturally could produce a similar site. In 2010 Jeffrey Schwartz and colleagues argued from teeth that many of the remains were of prenatal or newborn infants, a profile matching natural deaths. Patricia Smith and colleagues replied in 2011 that ages clustered at one to two months, which fits sacrifice better, and the exchange continued in the journal Antiquity. The balance of recent scholarship leans toward real child sacrifice, at least on some occasions, while the frequency and the share of burials that were offerings remain disputed.

title: When the Gods of the Americas Fell
description: Quetzalcoatl and a conquest myth, Huitzilopochtli's fall, and what Nahua Christians kept

concepts.title: Was Cortés Taken for Quetzalcoatl?
concepts.contentHtml:
Quetzalcoatl, "feathered serpent" in Nahuatl (from quetzalli, a long green tail feather, and coatl, snake), is one of the oldest gods of Mesoamerica. Feathered serpents decorate a temple at Teotihuacan built around 200 CE, and by Aztec times Quetzalcoatl was linked with the wind (as Ehecatl), priesthood, learning and the planet Venus. Separate legends told of Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, a priest-king of Tollan (Tula) who was driven out and went east.

A famous story says that when Hernán Cortés landed in 1519, the Mexica ruler Moctezuma II believed he was Quetzalcoatl returning in the year Ce Acatl, "One Reed", and so failed to resist. The sources do not support this well. Cortés's own letter to Charles V of 1520 reports a speech in which Moctezuma speaks of an ancestral lord who went away and whose descendants were expected to return, but it never names Quetzalcoatl. Historians such as Matthew Restall read the speech as courtly formality, reshaped by Cortés into a surrender that served his legal position. The explicit identification of Cortés with the god appears in accounts written decades later, above all the Florentine Codex, compiled under the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún from Nahua informants.

Scholars including Susan Gillespie, Camilla Townsend and Restall argue that the returning-god story grew after the conquest. It flattered Spaniards, who liked to think they had been received as gods, and it gave some Nahua writers an explanation of defeat in terms of omens and fate. The image of a fair-skinned Quetzalcoatl awaiting his return is a still later embroidery. Some scholars think a pre-conquest legend of Topiltzin's return may have existed, but its attachment to Cortés is a post-conquest product.

concepts.title: Huitzilopochtli and the Fall of Tenochtitlan
concepts.contentHtml:
Huitzilopochtli, usually translated "Hummingbird of the South" or "Hummingbird on the Left", was the patron god of the Mexica, who by their own tradition founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 and later built the Aztec empire. In their myth he was born fully armed on Coatepec, Serpent Mountain, to defend his mother Coatlicue against his sister Coyolxauhqui and the four hundred southern stars; he cut his sister apart and threw her down the mountain. His cult of sun and war required captives for sacrifice.

The Templo Mayor at the center of Tenochtitlan carried twin shrines, one for Huitzilopochtli and one for the rain god Tlaloc. In 1978 electricity workers in Mexico City struck a great carved stone disk showing the dismembered Coyolxauhqui, lying at the foot of Huitzilopochtli's stairs just as the myth placed her. The find launched the Templo Mayor Project under Eduardo Matos Moctezuma. Since 2015, excavations nearby have exposed part of the Huei Tzompantli, the great skull rack described by Spanish witnesses, with more than 600 skulls counted by 2020, including some of women and children.

The scale of sacrifice is debated. A colonial source gives 80,400 victims at the temple's rededication in 1487, a figure most historians regard as greatly exaggerated; the archaeology confirms large-scale killing without supporting such totals. Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521 to Cortés and his far more numerous Indigenous allies, above all Tlaxcalans, after a siege made worse by smallpox. The Templo Mayor was demolished and its stones reused, and the cathedral of Mexico City rose beside its ruins. In the late 1530s Spanish church investigators were still trying to trace hidden sacred bundles, including Huitzilopochtli's.

concepts.title: What Survived: Tonantzin, Nepantla and the Dead
concepts.contentHtml:
Conversion in New Spain was fast on the surface and slow underneath. Franciscan friars arrived in 1524, baptized Nahuas by the thousands and destroyed images, but they also learned Nahuatl and had to put Christian ideas into words that already carried meanings. The historian Louise Burkhart has shown how the terms the friars chose shaded the doctrine Nahuas actually heard. The Dominican Diego Durán recorded a Nahua man who, rebuked for mixing old and new practices, answered that his people were still nepantla, "in the middle".

The clearest case is Tepeyac, a hill north of Mexico City. Sahagún complained in the later 16th century that Native people there called the Virgin Tonantzin, "our revered mother", the name of a goddess formerly honored at the site. There the cult of the Virgin of Guadalupe grew. The story of her appearance to the Nahua Juan Diego in 1531 was first published in full by Miguel Sánchez in 1648, and in Nahuatl in 1649; its historicity is debated, and the church canonized Juan Diego in 2002.

Much that looks pre-Hispanic is a blend with a long colonial and modern history. The Day of the Dead joins the Catholic feasts of All Saints and All Souls with Indigenous practices, while the Mexica festivals for the dead fell at other times of year; the elegant skeleton later called La Catrina comes from the engraver José Guadalupe Posada around 1910. In many Indigenous communities, from Nahua villages to highland Maya towns such as San Juan Chamula, saints have taken on older responsibilities for rain, maize and mountains. Scholars now generally describe this as local Christianity in its own right rather than paganism in disguise.

title: The Norse Gods: Conversion and Revival
description: How Scandinavia became Christian, how we know its gods, and who worships them now

concepts.title: Kings, Runestones and the Althing
concepts.contentHtml:
Christianity reached Scandinavia over nearly three centuries, mostly through kings. The Frankish monk Ansgar preached at the Swedish trading town of Birka around 830 with little lasting result. At Jelling, in about 965, Harald Bluetooth raised a runestone boasting that he "won for himself all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian". In Norway, Olaf Tryggvason (r. 995 to 1000) and Olaf Haraldsson pressed conversion by force; the second fell at Stiklestad in 1030 and was soon venerated as Saint Olaf. Sweden held out longest. In the 1070s Adam of Bremen, a hostile writer who never went there, described a temple at Uppsala with images of Thor, Wodan and Fricco. For a time the faiths overlapped: a soapstone mold from Denmark could cast both crosses and Thor's hammers.

Iceland, settled from about 870, had no king. Its chieftains met each summer at the Althing, founded about 930. By the late 990s a Christian party, backed by Olaf Tryggvason, faced the pagans, and at the assembly of 999 or 1000 the two sides nearly declared separate laws. The priest Ari Thorgilsson, writing his Íslendingabók ("Book of the Icelanders") around 1122 to 1133, says the pagan lawspeaker Thorgeir was asked to decide. He lay under his cloak a day and a night without speaking, then warned that if they divided the law they would divide the peace, and ruled that all must be Christian and baptized. Exposure of infants and eating horse meat stayed legal for a time, and private sacrifice was allowed if no one witnessed it; Ari says these concessions were abolished a few years later.

A popular tale says Thorgeir then threw his idols into the waterfall Goðafoss. It is not in Ari or any medieval source and appears to be a 19th-century invention.

concepts.title: Snorri's Edda: Pagan Gods in a Christian Book
concepts.contentHtml:
Most of what people know about Odin, Thor, Loki and Ragnarök comes from Icelandic books written by Christians two centuries after the conversion. The Prose Edda was composed around 1220 by Snorri Sturluson (1179 to 1241), a rich chieftain, poet and twice lawspeaker of the Althing, as a handbook for poets who needed the old myths to understand the metaphors of skaldic verse. The Poetic Edda is a collection of anonymous poems preserved mainly in the Codex Regius, a manuscript written around 1270. Some of its poems may be centuries older than the manuscript, but dating them is contested.

Snorri frames the gods carefully. His Prologue explains them in the manner of euhemerism: the Æsir were men from Troy, whose leader Odin brought them north, where they were later worshiped as gods. In Gylfaginning a Swedish king questions three mysterious figures who tell him the myths, and at the end their hall vanishes, leaving the reader unsure what was illusion. Snorri also tidied scattered traditions into a system, and some of his details, including parts of the Ragnarök story and the portrait of Baldr, may reflect Christian influence. Scholars disagree about how much.

Other evidence exists but is scattered: skaldic poems composed in the Viking Age, runestones, place-names such as Odense ("Odin's sanctuary"), outside observers such as the Roman Tacitus and the Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan, the Danish historian Saxo Grammaticus writing in Latin around 1200, and the archaeology of cult buildings such as the one excavated at Uppåkra in southern Sweden. Together they point to a religion more varied and local than Snorri's orderly pantheon.

concepts.title: Ásatrú Returns, and a Fight over Its Meaning
concepts.contentHtml:
Organized worship of the Norse gods returned in the 20th century. In Iceland the farmer and poet Sveinbjörn Beinteinsson and a few others founded the Ásatrúarfélagið (the Ásatrú Fellowship) in 1972, and the state registered it as a religious organization in 1973. It now has more than 5,000 registered members, and since 2015 it has been building a temple on the Öskjuhlíð hill in Reykjavík, often described as the first in Iceland since the Viking Age. Its leaders call it a nature-centered religion without dogma, and its high priest has said publicly that members need not take the myths literally. Similar groups, often called heathens, exist across Europe and North America.

The revival also inherited a darker history. German nationalists and then the Nazis used runes and Germanic myth as racial emblems; the SS insignia was built from a rune. Since the 1970s a strand of North American heathenry called folkish has held that the religion belongs by ancestry to people of northern European descent. The Asatru Folk Assembly declared in 2016 that its membership was limited to people of European descent, and the Southern Poverty Law Center lists it as a hate group. Racist "Wotanism" was promoted by David Lane, a member of the 1980s white-supremacist terrorist group The Order.

Most heathen organizations reject this. In 2016 many groups signed Declaration 127, named for a stanza of the poem Hávamál about speaking out against evil, refusing to associate with the Asatru Folk Assembly. The Icelandic fellowship and the American organization The Troth are open to anyone regardless of ancestry. Symbols such as Thor's hammer are worn by many heathens with no such politics, so researchers stress that context decides what a symbol means.

concepts.title: Absorbed: Egyptian Gods Outlive Egypt
concepts.contentHtml:
Egyptian gods rarely died outright; they merged. Priests combined deities into composite forms: Amun of Thebes joined the sun god Ra as Amun-Ra, king of the gods in the New Kingdom, and Ptah, Sokar and Osiris were worshiped together as Ptah-Sokar-Osiris. Hathor and Isis shared so many titles and images that late depictions can be hard to tell apart. Egyptologists call this syncretism. It let a god take on a rival's worshipers and functions without either cult having to lose.

Greek rule after Alexander added another layer. Under Ptolemy I (r. 305 to 282 BCE) the cult of Serapis was promoted at Alexandria, joining the Memphite god Osiris-Apis to the bearded look of a Greek Zeus or Hades, so that both populations could approach him. Greeks also practiced interpretatio graeca, reading foreign gods as versions of their own: Herodotus equated Amun with Zeus, and the identification of Thoth with Hermes eventually produced Hermes Trismegistus, the "thrice-great" sage of later Greek esoteric writings. Isis spread across the Roman Empire as a universal goddess of countless names, with sanctuaries from Britain to the Black Sea.

The last datable hieroglyphic inscription was carved at the temple of Isis on the island of Philae in 394 CE, and the last known demotic graffito there dates to 452. Yet the gods lingered in other forms: in Coptic magical texts, in Greek alchemy and the Hermetic writings, and perhaps in Christian art, where some historians see the nursing Isis with the infant Horus behind early images of the Virgin and child, a link others consider overstated.

concepts.title: Gods into Planets and Allegories
concepts.contentHtml:
Greek and Roman gods outlived their cults partly by becoming something else. One refuge was the sky. Babylonian astronomers had linked planets with gods, Marduk with Jupiter and Ishtar with Venus, and by the 4th century BCE Greeks named the planets after the matching Olympians: the "star of Zeus", the "star of Aphrodite". The Roman versions gave English Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. When the seven-day planetary week spread through the empire, Germanic speakers substituted their own gods, which is why Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday honor Tiw, Woden, Thor and Frigg. Astronomers kept the habit: an 11-year-old Oxford girl, Venetia Burney, suggested the name Pluto in 1930.

Another refuge was allegory. In the 6th century BCE Theagenes of Rhegium is said to have read Homer's battling gods as natural elements in conflict. Stoic writers such as Cornutus explained Zeus as the cosmos and Hera as the air. Around 300 BCE Euhemerus argued, in a travel romance about an imaginary island, that the gods had been great kings deified after death. Christian writers such as Lactantius welcomed this, since it turned Jupiter into a dead man.

Medieval and Renaissance Christians kept the gods busy as moral emblems, astrological powers and ornaments of learning, in works from Fulgentius's Mythologies to the 14th-century Ovide moralisé and Boccaccio's Genealogy of the Pagan Gods. The art historian Jean Seznec traced this story in The Survival of the Pagan Gods (1940; English translation 1953). His conclusion: the gods never vanished from Christian Europe; they changed jobs.

concepts.title: Obituaries and Revivals
concepts.contentHtml:
In "Memorial Service", collected in Prejudices: Third Series (1922), the American journalist H. L. Mencken asked, "Where is the grave-yard of dead gods?" and answered with a mock funeral roll: Jupiter, Huitzilopochtli, Quetzalcoatl, Baal, Astarte, Amon-Re, Isis, Osiris, Odin, Marduk and well over a hundred more, ending with "And all are dead." His real target was the certainty of believers in his own day. His scholarship was loose. His sacrifice totals for the Aztec gods have no reliable source, he credited Gaulish gods such as Epona to the ancient Irish, and his list includes places, such as Mictlan, the Aztec underworld, as if they were gods.

A century later, some of his dead have worshipers again. Modern revivals sit on a spectrum. Reconstructionists try to rebuild a specific historical religion from ancient sources and modern scholarship: Hellenic polytheists in Greece, whose religion won legal status as a "known religion" in 2017; Kemetic groups devoted to Egyptian gods; Lithuanian Romuva; Slavic Rodnovery; heathens working from the Eddas. Eclectic movements such as Wicca blend sources freely instead. Reconstructionists face a hard problem: the old religions survive mostly in texts written by elites, outsiders or enemies, so every revival involves choice and invention, which practitioners themselves discuss openly.

Whether a revived Odin is the same god is a theological question, not a historical one. The historical pattern across this topic is clearer. Cults have been cut off by decree (Amun briefly under Akhenaten, Rome's public gods under Theodosius), by conquest (Huitzilopochtli), by negotiated vote (Iceland) and by slow absorption (Egypt). In every case the names, images and stories proved harder to kill than the worship.
